choices.text: The book was not found
choices.why: That is 404.

choices.text: The request is still being processed and will finish later
choices.why: That would be 202 Accepted.

choices.text: The method is not allowed there
choices.why: That is 405.

choices.text: `/v1/books_by_author?author=2&action=list`
choices.why: An action in the query string is a verb in disguise.

prompt: A client sends a PATCH that adds 1 to a counter, the connection drops, and it is not sure the server got it. Why may it not simply resend?
hint: What does HTTP promise about PATCH?

choices.text: PATCH is not safe
choices.why: No writing method is safe; PUT is not safe either and may be resent.

choices.text: A second copy would add 1 again: this patch is not idempotent
choices.why: Right. HTTP does not promise idempotence for PATCH, and this one lacks it.

choices.text: PATCH bodies are lost when a connection drops
choices.why: The worry is the opposite: that it arrived.

choices.text: The server answers 409 to any repeated request
choices.why: Nothing in HTTP does that by itself.

choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Telling clients by e-mail to update the same day
choices.why: Their code breaks on deploy whatever the e-mail says.

choices.text: Keeping `price_cents` in the database
choices.why: The database is not what clients read; the representation is.

choices.text: Answering 301 from `/v1` to `/v2`
choices.why: That sends them the new shape they cannot read.

prompt: `jq -n '39.90 * 3'` prints `119.69999999999999`, and so does Python. Why?

choices.text: jq keeps numbers as text until it prints them
choices.why: It multiplies a double; the text is gone once it does arithmetic.

choices.text: The 3 is read as a float and spoils it
choices.why: 3 is exact in binary. The trouble is 39.90.

choices.text: 39.90 has no exact value in binary floating point
choices.why: Right. The error shows as soon as it is multiplied, which is why money travels as integer cents.

choices.text: Both tools have a rounding bug that newer versions fix
choices.why: It is how binary floating point works, not a bug in either tool.

prompt: A client sends `catalogue.py` a book with `"year": 1891.0`. What does `book.schema.json` make of that year?

choices.text: It passes as an integer
choices.why: Right. JSON Schema's `integer` is a number with no fractional part, and 1891.0 has none, as `3990.0` had none.

choices.text: It is refused: `integer` excludes a number written with a decimal point
choices.why: That is the definition many expect. JSON Schema's is about the value, and the lesson's `3990.0` passed.

choices.text: It is refused because a year has to be sent as a string
choices.why: The schema asks for an integer; the string `"1891"` is what it refuses.

choices.text: It passes once `jsonschema` rounds it to 1891
choices.why: A validator changes nothing in the body; 1891.0 already has no fractional part.

prompt: A client copies the catalogue page by page with `offset`. Between its first and second page, somebody deletes a book that was on the first page. What does the copy end up with?

choices.text: A 404 for the deleted book on the second page
choices.why: An offset counts positions; it does not look the deleted row up.

choices.text: The same book twice
choices.why: That is what an insert does, by moving rows back. A delete moves them forward.

choices.text: An error from the server, since the offset now skips a missing row
choices.why: Neither case produces an error, and that is the danger.

choices.text: A gap: every later row moved forward one place, so one book is skipped without an error
choices.why: Right. The offset's second page starts one row further on than it did, and the row that slid into the first page is never fetched.

prompt: A client asks `catalogue.py` for `?limit=500` and gets a 400 saying `limit is a whole number from 1 to 100`. Why is that better than quietly sending 100?

choices.text: Sending 100 rows would be slower than refusing
choices.why: Speed is not the point; the refusal is about what the client believes it got.

choices.text: A client given fewer rows than it asked for has to notice
choices.why: Right. A refusal is impossible to misread; a limit lowered in silence is easy to miss.

choices.text: A 400 makes the client retry with the same limit until it works
choices.why: The same request gets the same 400; the client has to change the limit.

choices.text: The cursor in `next` breaks when a page is shorter than asked
choices.why: The `next` link works for any page size; it carries the sort and the last row.

prompt: shelf's documentation says nothing about the order `/v1/books` lists books in, and a team wants to change it. By Hyrum's law, what should it check first?

choices.text: Whether any client relies on the order, by asking the clients
choices.why: Right. With enough users, every observable behaviour is depended on by somebody, documented or not.

choices.text: Whether the documentation mentions the order
choices.why: That is the question Hyrum's law replaces: what clients use, not what was written.

choices.text: Whether the new order still passes `book.schema.json`
choices.why: That schema checks a book a client sends, not the order of a list.

choices.text: Whether the change has to go out as a new version, under `/v2`
choices.why: That follows from the answer; first you need to know whether anybody reads the order.

prompt: `catalogue.py` was sent `{"title": "", "year": "1891", "price_cents": 39.90}`. How many entries did the `errors` member of its problem details carry?
Match each thing an API sends to the way the catalogue's contract makes it travel in JSON.

an RFC 3339 string with an offset
a link to it, or base64 in a string

prompt: Which of these does a cursor made by `catalogue.py` hold? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: the sort it was made for
choices.why: Right. That is why a cursor from one sort is refused in another.

choices.text: the number of the page
choices.why: That would be an offset again; a cursor names a row, not a position.

choices.text: the last row's value for that sort
choices.why: Right. The next page starts after that value.

choices.text: a signature that keeps the client from reading it
choices.why: It is base64, which anybody decodes; opaque does not mean secret.

choices.text: the last row's id
choices.why: Right. It breaks ties, so two books with the same value come back in the same order.

prompt: Your dashboard counts 4xx and 5xx answers from `graph.py`. After a deploy, every `setStock` call fails on the database's `CHECK`. What does the dashboard show?

choices.text: A rise in 500s, one per failed write
choices.why: The query ran, so the answer is 200; the failure is inside the body.

choices.text: A rise in 400s, since the stock value was invalid
choices.why: `graph.py` answers 400 when nothing ran: a parse, validation or depth failure. Here the query ran.

choices.text: Nothing unusual: each failure arrives as a 200 with `errors` beside the data
choices.why: Right. A 200 only says the query ran; the server has to count the errors in its bodies itself.

choices.text: A 409 for each write that clashed
choices.why: GraphQL does not turn a failed field into a status code.

prompt: A team changes `Author.country` from `String!` to `String`, because some authors have no country recorded. Who is at risk?
hint: Which direction of the `!` is safe?

choices.text: Nobody: loosening a type is the safe direction
choices.why: It is the opposite. Making a nullable field non-null is safe; taking the promise away breaks whoever relied on it.

choices.text: Clients that wrote code trusting `country` is never null
choices.why: Right. `!` is a promise a client may build on, and removing it breaks that code.

choices.text: Only the server, whose resolvers must now produce a value for every single author
choices.why: With `String` the resolver may return null; the server's job got easier, not harder.

choices.text: Clients that do not ask for `country` at all
choices.why: A field nobody selects is never resolved for them, so its type cannot reach them.

prompt: The schema says `book(id: ID!): Book`. A client asks `{ book(id: 99) { title } }` and there is no book 99. What comes back?

choices.text: A 404, the way `rest.py` would answer
choices.why: GraphQL has one address; a missing object is data, not a status.

choices.text: A 400 saying the id is invalid
choices.why: `99` is a valid `ID`. It simply matches nothing.

choices.text: An empty object under `book`
choices.why: An object would have to carry `title`, which is `String!`; there is no book to give it one.

choices.text: `null` under `book`
choices.why: Right. `Book` has no `!`, and the schema uses that for an id that matches nothing.

prompt: A CDN is put in front of `graph.py`, and it never serves a read from its cache. Why?

choices.text: Every read is a `POST` to one address
choices.why: Right. A cache keys on method and address and in practice stores no `POST`; the request line says nothing about what was asked.

choices.text: GraphQL answers carry no `Content-Type`, so a cache refuses them
choices.why: They are `application/json` like any other answer; the trouble is in the request.

choices.text: The answers change too often, since each client picks its own fields
choices.why: Different shapes would cache fine if the address said which shape. It does not.

choices.text: The answers are too large for a CDN to keep around
choices.why: Size is not the issue; a GraphQL answer is the size of the screen.

prompt: Why does writing `book(id: $id)` with a variable, rather than `book(id: 4)`, matter to persisted queries?

choices.text: Variables are checked against their declared types, and literal values are not
choices.why: Both are checked against the schema; that is not what persistence needs.

choices.text: A literal value makes the query too deep for `MAX_DEPTH`
choices.why: Depth counts fields, not values.

choices.text: The text is then the same for every book, so the server registers it once
choices.why: Right. A persisted query is a fixed text the server knows; only the variables change between requests.

choices.text: A query with variables runs without resolvers
choices.why: Every field is resolved the same way; a variable only carries a value.

prompt: `graph.py` runs with `--batch`, and the shop has 100 books by 30 authors. How many SQL queries does `{ books { title author { name } } }` cost?
hint: One for the list, and then?

prompt: Match each type written in a schema to what it promises.

pairs.right: one object, never null
the list and its items may both be null
the list may be null, its items may not
always a list, with no null items

right_distractors: always a list, though an item may be null

prompt: Which of these are true of the data loader in `graph.py`? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: It gathers the ids asked for and fetches them with one `WHERE id IN (…)`
choices.why: Right. `load` collects the ids and `fetch` asks for them together.

choices.text: An id already promised in the same request is not fetched again
choices.why: Right. Author 1 was asked for once, where the plain resolver asked twice.

choices.text: It fixes the N+1 problem for the fields below it as well
choices.why: It fixes the field it was written for; `Author.books` still ran one query per author.

choices.text: It is shared between requests, so authors stay cached
choices.why: It lives for one request on purpose; shared, it would be a cache with questions of freshness and of who may see what.

choices.text: It lives for one request and is then thrown away
choices.why: Right. That is deliberate, and it keeps it from being a cache.

prompt: A till calls the warehouse with a 2-second deadline. 1.5 seconds in, the warehouse has to ask a supplier before it can answer. What deadline should its call to the supplier carry?

choices.text: A fresh 2 seconds, the same as the till's
choices.why: The supplier would go on working after the till had stopped waiting for the answer.

choices.text: What is left of the till's: about half a second
choices.why: Right. Passing on the remainder keeps the supplier from working for an answer nobody is waiting for.

choices.text: No deadline, since the supplier is an internal service
choices.why: gRPC sets no deadline unless you do, and a call without one may wait for ever on a server that stopped answering.

choices.text: Ten seconds, so that a slower supplier has room to finish
choices.why: The till gives up at two seconds; anything the supplier does after that is wasted.

prompt: A till sends `Reserve` with `copies: -2`. Which status fits?

choices.text: `INVALID_ARGUMENT`: no state of the shelf makes it valid
choices.why: Right. The request is wrong as it stands, whatever the stock.

choices.text: `FAILED_PRECONDITION`: the shelf is not in a state to give it
choices.why: That code says the request is fine and the system is not ready for it. No delivery makes -2 copies a reservation.

choices.text: `NOT_FOUND`: there is no such reservation
choices.why: `NOT_FOUND` is for a thing named that does not exist; the book here exists.

choices.text: `INTERNAL`: the database's `CHECK` would refuse it
choices.why: `INTERNAL` says the server broke. Here the server refuses the request before touching the database.

prompt: A delivery streams a box of 5 Dom Casmurro, then a box for an ISBN that does not exist. The call ends `NOT_FOUND`, and Dom Casmurro still has 10 copies. Why were the 5 not kept?

choices.text: gRPC undoes a client stream that ends in an error
choices.why: gRPC does nothing of the kind. A server that committed box by box would have kept the five.

choices.text: The client did not send the first box once the stream had failed
choices.why: The first box arrived and was applied before the second failed.

choices.text: The server ran the delivery in one transaction
choices.why: Right. `abort` raised inside the server's `with` block, and the first box was rolled back with the second.

choices.text: A client stream is answered at the end, so the server writes at the end too
choices.why: Answering at the end is about the reply. The server ran the first box's `UPDATE` before the second box failed.

prompt: A reporting service, built with the first `stock.proto`, reads a level from the next release, lowers `copies` by one and writes the message on. What happens to `location`?

choices.text: It is dropped, because the old code has no field for it
choices.why: An unknown field is not thrown away; old code that reads and writes a message keeps it.

choices.text: It becomes `title`, the field the old code expected
choices.why: That would happen to a field given number 2; `location` has 5.

choices.text: The decode fails, and the service refuses the message
choices.why: Nothing failed when the old `stock.proto` read the new bytes.

choices.text: It travels on as field 5, kept although the old code has no name for it
choices.why: Right. The re-encoded message still held `5: "A3"` with `copies` at 11.

pairs.right: a varint, for `int32`, `bool` or an enum
eight bytes, for a `double`

prompt: What does running on HTTP/2 give the warehouse's gRPC calls? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Many calls on one TCP connection, each its own stream
choices.why: Right. A channel opens one connection and sends every call on it.

choices.text: A watch open for an hour that does not hold up reservations on the same connection
choices.why: Right. Each call is a stream with its own frames.

choices.text: A status that a page's `fetch()` can read
choices.why: The status is in trailers, and `fetch()` gives a page no way to read them.

choices.text: Answers that HTTP caches keep, like a `GET`
choices.why: Every gRPC call is a `POST`, and caches do not keep those.

choices.text: Messages flowing in either direction until one side says it has finished
choices.why: Right. The same framing is what makes a stream in either direction possible.

prompt: A metadata key that carries bytes rather than text ends in ___.
The bridge waits up to 2 seconds for the distributor. The shop's checkout calls the bridge with a timeout of 1 second. What goes wrong on a day the distributor is slow?

choices.text: Checkout gives up first, and the bridge's answer goes nowhere
choices.why: Right. Each layer's timeout has to be shorter than the one above it, or the lower layer's answer reaches nobody.

choices.text: Little: the shorter outer timeout just makes the chain fail sooner
choices.why: The outer layer gives up first, and whatever the bridge learns afterwards is lost.

choices.text: The bridge retries until the checkout's second is over
choices.why: The bridge does not retry; it waits once, up to two seconds.

choices.text: The distributor refuses calls that arrive with under 2 s left
choices.why: A SOAP call carries no deadline; passing one along is gRPC's habit, not this protocol's.

prompt: Which costs the shelf more: a distributor that is down, or one that is slow?
hint: Look at how long each took to fail.

choices.text: A down one: each request waits for the connection to time out
choices.why: A refused connection fails at once; the bridge answered 502 after 0.003 s.

choices.text: The same, since each ends in a gateway status
choices.why: The statuses are alike; the time spent and the threads held are not.

choices.text: A slow one: each request holds a thread for the full two seconds
choices.why: Right. That is the cost a circuit breaker exists to cut.

choices.text: A down one, because a 502 sets off the shelf's own alarms
choices.why: 502 is a gateway code precisely so that the shelf's alarms on 500 stay quiet.

prompt: `bridge.py` builds its zeep client from `distributor.wsdl` in the project, rather than from `?wsdl` on the live service. What does that buy?

choices.text: Faster orders, since each one skips a trip for the contract
choices.why: The bridge builds its client once, at start-up, either way; the reason is in another option.

choices.text: It starts with the distributor down, and their changes wait for a reviewed diff
choices.why: Right. A change on their side cannot reach the code until somebody replaces the file and reads the diff.

choices.text: Protection from the distributor's faults, which the local copy maps to the shelf's own statuses
choices.why: The `FAULTS` table does that mapping; the WSDL says nothing about `E100` or `E200`.

choices.text: Its values arrive as strings, which are safer than zeep's types
choices.why: zeep converts to the types the schema declares, whichever copy it read.

prompt: With `use_digest=True`, the `Password` element differs in every message although the password does not. Why?

choices.text: zeep encrypts it with a new key for each message
choices.why: Nothing is encrypted; a digest is one-way, and its inputs vary.

choices.text: The server sends a fresh password before each call
choices.why: The password is the same; the server sends nothing before the call.

choices.text: It is the password hashed with a salt the server keeps
choices.why: That is how a password is stored; this digest forces the server to keep the password itself.

choices.text: A nonce and the time are digested with it
choices.why: Right. The nonce and `Created` change, so the digest changes, and a server can refuse a nonce it has seen.

prompt: A server checks a valid XML Signature over an `Amount` element, then reads the first `Amount` it finds in the message. What is the flaw?
hint: Which element did the signature cover?

choices.text: The first `Amount` could be an unsigned copy placed beside the signed one
choices.why: Right. Code has to read the element the signature covers, found through the signature.

choices.text: The signature should be checked after the value is read
choices.why: The order is not the problem; which element is read is.

choices.text: A signature proves who sent it, not that it was unchanged
choices.why: It proves both: that the signed parts were not changed, and who signed them.

choices.text: A signature breaks when a gateway passes the message on
choices.why: It survives gateways and archives; that is its advantage over TLS.

prompt: A file in an older project opens with `swagger: "2.0"`. What is it?

choices.text: A configuration file for Swagger UI
choices.why: Swagger UI reads a document; this line is the document's own first line, naming its format.

choices.text: The old format, from before it was renamed OpenAPI
choices.why: Right. 2.0 is the last version called Swagger, and a tool that reads 3.1 may refuse it.

choices.text: Version 2 of the API it describes, the one served under `/v2`
choices.why: The line names the specification's version, not the API's, and not `info.version` either.

choices.text: An OpenAPI 3.1 document saved by the Swagger Editor, which names it after itself
choices.why: A 3.1 document opens with `openapi: 3.1.0`, whoever wrote it; tools may still refuse the other.

prompt: You delete `~/shelf/.venv`. Which of this lesson's commands stops working?

choices.text: `python3 check_contract.py`, because it imports `jsonschema`
choices.why: It runs with Ubuntu's `python3`, which imports the `jsonschema` apt installed.

choices.text: `python3 rest.py`, because the venv replaced the system's Python
choices.why: A venv leaves the system's Python alone; plain `python3` is Ubuntu's.

choices.text: Any Python command, until the venv is made again
choices.why: The venv was not activated in this lesson, and plain `python3` does not use it.

choices.text: `.venv/bin/openapi-spec-validator`, with the rest of what pip downloaded into the venv
choices.why: Right. Deleting `.venv` removes everything the download brought, and nothing else on the machine notices.

prompt: A colleague's `openapi.yaml` adds `GET /authors`, which `rest.py` answers with 404, and `openapi-spec-validator` prints `OK`. What would catch the mistake?

choices.text: Running the validator with `--validation-errors all`
choices.why: That lists more errors of the same kind, and the validator does not look at `rest.py`.

choices.text: Rendering the document in Swagger UI and reading the page
choices.why: The page would show `GET /authors` as a perfectly good panel; it is drawn from the document.

choices.text: A contract test that sends `GET /authors`
choices.why: Right. Only a program holding the document and the running server at once sees the 404 the document does not list.

choices.text: Converting the YAML to JSON and passing it to `jq`
choices.why: That reads the document as data; it does not ask the server anything.

prompt: A code-first team generates its document from the handlers. Why commit the generated document to the repository?

choices.text: So a change to the contract shows up as a diff in the pull request
choices.why: Right. Otherwise a rename in a model class changes the contract with nobody deciding it should.

choices.text: Because the framework needs the file to serve Swagger UI
choices.why: FastAPI builds the document at run time and serves the page; the file in the repository is for reviewers.

choices.text: So the code generator can rebuild the handlers from it
choices.why: In code-first the handlers are what people write; the document is the output.

choices.text: Because a committed document lists the errors the handlers do not declare
choices.why: Committing it does not change its content: an undeclared 500 is still missing.

prompt: A front-end team wants to start building against shelf's next API before the back end has a line of code. Which arrangement does the lesson describe for that?

choices.text: Code-first, so the document is ready as soon as the handlers exist
choices.why: Then the document arrives with the code, which is what the team cannot wait for.

choices.text: Generating a server stub and letting it answer for the back end
choices.why: A stub has empty handlers; somebody still writes every body before it answers anything useful.

choices.text: Swagger UI's Try it out, aimed at the draft
choices.why: Try it out sends real requests to the server in `servers`, which does not exist yet.

choices.text: Design-first, and a mock server built from the draft
choices.why: Right. A mock server such as Prism answers with the draft's examples, so clients start the day the document is agreed; nothing else has to exist.

prompt: `rest.py` does some things that shelf's `openapi.yaml` leaves out on purpose. Which of these are left out? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: the 405 that `DELETE /v1/books` gets
choices.why: Right. A method the document does not list is one a client should not send.

choices.text: the 409 for an ISBN another book has
choices.why: It is there, as `Conflict` under `components/responses`.

choices.text: version 2, under `/v2`
choices.why: Right. Describing both would put a version in front of every path; a second version is better off in a document of its own.

choices.text: the 204 with no body after a delete
choices.why: It is there: a response with a `description` and no `content`.

choices.text: the 501 Python's library sends to `OPTIONS`
choices.why: Right. Nobody chose it, so nobody wrote it down; the contract test found it.

prompt: An API answers 401 when a signed-in user asks for something they are not allowed to do. What happens to a client that follows the rules for a 401?

choices.text: It shows the refusal and stops
choices.why: That is what a client does with a 403. Told 401, it believes a login will help.

choices.text: It signs in again, asks again, and goes round a loop
choices.why: Right. The server should have said 403: it knows who this is, and the answer is no.

choices.text: It resends the same request with the same token
choices.why: The rule for a 401 is to log in again or ask the user, not to resend the credential that failed.

choices.text: It falls back to Basic, the other scheme the challenge offered
choices.why: Another scheme proves the same name, and the answer stays 401.

prompt: Another API's keys are 43 random characters and nothing else. One is pushed by mistake to a public repository. What does it lack that a `keys.py` key has?

choices.text: A hash, since a key with no prefix is stored as it was sent
choices.why: Any random string can be hashed; the prefix only finds the row.

choices.text: Strength: it is the prefix that makes a key hard to guess
choices.why: The prefix is not secret; the random part is what nobody can guess.

choices.text: A shape secret scanners know, so the owner is warned
choices.why: Right. A bare random string looks like any other to them; `shelf_2ff69109` is recognisable in a repository, a log or a ticket.

choices.text: An expiry, which `keys.py` writes into the prefix

prompt: Ana changes her password because she thinks it leaked. What should the server do with the tokens she already holds?

choices.text: Keep them: a token is not the password
choices.why: Whoever took her password may already hold a token, and it is her while it lasts.

choices.text: Let them run out within the hour
choices.why: An hour is long for somebody who has one. Expiry is for leaks nobody knows about.

choices.text: Rehash them with her new password
choices.why: Tokens are hashed with SHA-256 alone; the password is not part of them.

choices.text: Delete every row of hers in `tokens`, logging her out everywhere
choices.why: Right. `DELETE FROM tokens WHERE user_id = 1` is revocation with a wider `WHERE`.

prompt: A 401's Bearer challenge carries `error="invalid_token"`. What does that add for the client?

choices.text: A token came and was not accepted, so it should log in again
choices.why: Right. It is different from no token at all, and the client does not need to know why.

choices.text: The token expired, rather than being revoked
choices.why: It does not say which: expired, revoked and never issued look the same.

choices.text: The token is valid but not allowed to do this
choices.why: That would be a 403, which carries no challenge.

choices.text: The token was sent in the wrong header
choices.why: It arrived in `Authorization`; the server hashed it and found no row.

prompt: `by_token` never calls `compare_digest`, and still leaks nothing through its timing. Why?

choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so; the point is what is compared, not how.

choices.text: It looks up the token's hash rather than the token itself
choices.why: Right. A caller cannot steer a hash's first characters by changing the token, so a timing difference teaches nothing.

choices.text: Tokens are too short for timing to show
choices.why: Keys are 43 random characters as well, and `keys.py` still compares them with `compare_digest`.

choices.text: Its refusal is slowed down by running scrypt first
choices.why: scrypt runs for passwords. A token gets one SHA-256.

prompt: `sessions.py` leaves `Domain` out of its cookie. On a shop at `shop.example.com`, a colleague adds `Domain=example.com`. What changes?

choices.text: Every `*.example.com` gets it, other people's hosts included

choices.text: The cookie stops reaching `shop.example.com` itself

choices.text: The browser drops it, as it drops a `Secure` cookie over HTTP

prompt: A server answers a login at `/v1/login` with `Set-Cookie: sid=…` and no `Path`. The client then asks for `/me`. What happens?

choices.text: The cookie goes everywhere on the host, `Path=/` being the default
choices.why: The default comes from the address that set the cookie, here `/v1`.

choices.text: `/me` gets no cookie: it was scoped to `/v1`
choices.why: Right. That is why `sessions.py` writes `Path=/` out.

choices.text: The browser refuses to keep a cookie that names no path

choices.text: The cookie is sent, but the server ignores it outside `/v1`
choices.why: The server would look the id up anywhere; it is the client that leaves the cookie off.

prompt: A server accepts `HS256` and `RS256`, lets each token's header pick, and has published its RSA public key. What can an attacker do?

choices.why: Neither algorithm encrypts; anybody holding a JWT reads its payload.

choices.text: Work out the private key from the published public one
choices.why: The public key does not give away the private one. The danger is elsewhere.

choices.text: Sign an HS256 token with the public key, which the server then uses as an HMAC key
choices.why: Right. A public key is not a secret, and here it signs tokens the server believes. Name exactly one algorithm.

prompt: An access token carries `"role": "editor"`. An administrator takes ana's editor role away. What does her current token say?

choices.text: No role, since a payload may not carry permissions

choices.text: `editor`, until its `exp`
choices.why: Right. A token holding permissions keeps saying the old thing until it expires.

prompt: Which of these tokens does `tokens.py`'s `verify` refuse? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A correctly signed token with no `exp`
choices.why: Right. `verify` requires all seven claims, so a missing one is refused rather than waved through.

choices.text: A token whose header says `"alg": "none"`
choices.why: Right. `algorithms=["HS256"]` leaves `none` off the list.

choices.text: A token issued 310 seconds ago with a 300-second life
choices.why: Its `exp` passed 10 seconds ago, inside the 30 seconds of leeway; `/me` accepted it.

choices.text: A token whose `jti` is in the `revoked` table
choices.why: Right. The last check reads the denylist on every request.

choices.text: An access token from a sign-in whose refresh token was then reused
choices.why: Reuse deletes the refresh tokens; the access token already issued still worked.

prompt: A client skips the check of `state` when the browser comes back to its callback. What can a page somewhere else now do?

choices.text: Read the access token from the browser's history
choices.why: In the code flow the token does not pass through the browser; `state` is about a code being forced in.

choices.text: Exchange your code without the PKCE verifier
choices.why: The verifier still guards the exchange; `state` is about a code arriving that the client did not ask for.

choices.text: Slip its own code into your sign-in
choices.why: Right. Your browser arrives at the callback with a code the page chose, and the app attaches somebody else's account to your session.

choices.text: Change the scope the person agreed to on the consent screen
choices.why: Consent happens on the authorization server's own page, which the callback check does not touch.

prompt: A phone app uses PKCE with the method `plain` instead of `S256`. What does it give up?

choices.text: Its refresh tokens, which `plain` does not allow
choices.why: PKCE protects the code exchange; refresh tokens are another matter.

choices.text: The browser carries the verifier itself, so a stolen code comes with its proof
choices.why: Right. With `plain` the challenge is the verifier, so the hash that cannot be run backwards is gone, and that was all PKCE had.

choices.text: Exact matching of the `redirect_uri`, which `S256` switches on
choices.why: The address is compared exactly whatever the PKCE method; the two checks are separate.

choices.text: Little: with no client secret to protect, the two methods give a phone app the same protection
choices.why: Without a secret, PKCE is the only protection a phone app's code has, and `plain` hands its proof to the browser.

prompt: A SAML assertion arrives with a certificate embedded in its signature. Which certificate should the service provider verify it with?

choices.text: The identity provider's, from the metadata exchanged at setup
choices.why: Right. A message brings whatever certificate it likes; the one held before every sign-in is the one an attacker did not choose.

choices.text: The one embedded in the message, after checking that it parses
choices.why: A forger embeds a certificate of their own, and their signature verifies against it.

choices.text: Whichever one the browser's certificate store trusts
choices.why: The browser merely carries the form; the trust was set up between the two servers.

choices.text: The service provider's own certificate, used to sign its request back
choices.why: The identity provider signed the assertion, so it is the identity provider's key that has to check it.

prompt: Why did the implicit grant exist in the first place?

choices.text: To spare servers the cost of a second request
choices.why: Cost was not the reason; when it was designed, a browser app could not count on making that second request.

choices.text: Because access tokens were too long for a form post
choices.why: Length was not the issue; the issue was which origin a page could call.

choices.text: To give phone apps a flow without a redirect
choices.why: The implicit grant was a redirect, with the token in it.

choices.text: JavaScript in a page could not count on being allowed to call `/token` on another origin
choices.why: Right. CORS made that call ordinary and PKCE made it safe without a secret, so the reason is gone.

prompt: Somebody copies `idp-key.pem` off the machine. What can they do with it?

choices.text: Read Ana's password from it

choices.text: Decrypt the access tokens that clients already hold
choices.why: The tokens are signed, not encrypted; their claims are readable with no key at all.

choices.text: Sign tokens that APIs trusting this server accept, for any user and scope
choices.why: Right. That file is all of the authorization server's authority, which is why a real one keeps it in a key store.

choices.text: Change the public key that `/jwks.json` publishes, and lock the clients out of it
choices.why: Publishing is the server's job; the copy lets them sign, which is worse.

prompt: A leak takes `shelf.db` and the server's files too, the pepper's key included. What does the pepper add against that attacker?
hint: Where is a pepper worth something?

choices.text: It keeps every hash safe, since the pepper is not in the database
choices.why: It was in the files that leaked; a key protects only while it stays secret.

choices.text: It doubles the cost of each guess, as a second salt would
choices.why: An HMAC is cheap, and the cost per guess is the hash's. A pepper is not a second salt.

choices.text: Nothing: each guess runs the HMAC with the stolen key first
choices.why: Right. A pepper earns its place only when the database leaks and the server's secrets do not.

choices.text: It forces the attacker to crack the pepper before any row
choices.why: The key was taken whole; there is nothing left to crack.

prompt: Somebody holding a leaked table wants one particular account's password. Compared with plain SHA-256, what does salted SHA-256 cost them per guess?

choices.text: About the same: over a million guesses a second
choices.why: Right. A salt makes each row its own job; it does not make one guess dearer. That is the cost factor's work.

choices.text: Twice as much, since the salt is hashed along with the password
choices.why: Mixing in a few more bytes barely changes SHA-256's time.

choices.text: As much as bcrypt, because each guess needs the secret salt
choices.why: The salt is not secret: it sits beside the hash, in plain sight.

choices.text: Too much to try, since the salt hides which hash belongs to whom
choices.why: The row still names its user; the salt only stops one guess serving many rows.

prompt: A team salts each password with the user's e-mail address. What is wrong with that?

choices.text: An e-mail address is too long to be a salt
choices.why: Length is not the trouble; being known in advance is.

choices.text: It is known before any leak, and the same on every site
choices.why: Right. A predictable salt lets the work be done in advance, and once for every site that used it.

choices.text: A salt has to be secret, and an e-mail is not
choices.why: A salt is not a secret. It has to be unique and random.

choices.text: Two users with one password still get one hash
choices.why: Their addresses differ, so their hashes differ; the flaw is elsewhere.

prompt: Why does `passwords.py` read the password from standard input rather than take it as a command-line argument?

choices.text: Standard input keeps it out of the shell's history
choices.why: The lesson's own `echo` into a pipe leaves it in the history.

choices.text: Argon2id refuses a password with spaces when it comes from the command line
choices.why: Argon2id hashes whatever string it is given, spaces included.

choices.text: Other users of the machine see a running command's arguments
choices.why: Right. The arguments of a running command are visible to every user of the machine.

prompt: The library's default, `m=102400 t=2 p=8`, took 181.533 ms, and `m=65536 t=2 p=1` took 192.576 ms. Why was the larger memory quicker?

choices.text: A UUID can be worked out from the order's date

choices.text: Customers lose the links to their orders when the ids change

prompt: Another API guards its admin functions with one check: a path starting with `/admin` needs an admin. A developer adds `GET /reports/customers`, which lists the customers. What happens?

choices.text: Anybody with a valid token gets in

choices.text: It answers 404 until it appears in the OpenAPI document
choices.why: The document describes routes; it does not switch them on.

prompt: In `orders.py`, a request's effective permissions are the role's set and the token's scopes joined with Python's set operator ___.

choices.why: It lets twice the limit through across a boundary.

choices.text: A sliding log

choices.text: A sliding window counter, two numbers per client

prompt: A sliding window counter sees a previous window whose requests all came in its first second. What does its estimate do to the client?

choices.why: That is the case of requests bunched at the end of the window, still inside the last ten seconds.

choices.text: It refuses the client when it still had room
choices.why: Right. The estimate counts a share of requests that are already outside the last ten seconds, so it is too high.

choices.text: It is exact, since the previous window is complete

choices.text: It drops the previous window and counts the current one alone

prompt: Why does the lesson compare `Content-Length` with a ceiling before a single byte of the body is read?

choices.text: Because a request rate limit counts the bytes as well

choices.text: So that `rest.py` can parse the JSON in pieces
choices.why: The ceiling is about whether to read at all, not about how to parse.

choices.text: A server that trusts the number reads whatever it is told into memory, and the work is done before any check

prompt: Four copies of an API share one Redis for their counters, at the price of a round trip on every request. For which limit does the lesson call that price worth paying?

choices.text: The login limit, since it is the smallest

prompt: A fixed window is changed so that each client's window starts at its own first request instead of on the clock. What does that fix?

choices.text: The `Retry-After`, which becomes exact

choices.text: The PATCH stays in the browser, like one from an unlisted origin
choices.why: Within the ten minutes there is no question in front of it, so it goes out.

choices.text: The server refuses the PATCH because the origin is off the list
choices.why: `secure.py` refuses nothing on `Origin`; it leaves the header out.

prompt: Why does a real site start `Strict-Transport-Security` at a few minutes rather than at a year?

choices.text: A browser that saw it refuses plain HTTP for the whole period
choices.why: Right. It is a promise that is hard to take back, so it grows once HTTPS is known to work everywhere.

choices.text: Browsers ignore a `max-age` over an hour on a first visit
choices.why: Browsers cap the preflight's `Max-Age`; nothing like that applies here.

choices.text: A short value makes the first visit safe as well
choices.why: The first visit is the gap HSTS leaves open; `preload` is what closes it.

choices.text: The certificate has to be renewed before `max-age` ends
choices.why: The two are unrelated; a renewed certificate keeps working under HSTS.

prompt: A cover download resolves the client's host name, checks that the address is public, then hands the URL to an HTTP library that resolves the name again and connects. What is the hole?

choices.text: Public addresses are where the cloud's metadata service lives
choices.why: It lives at 169.254.169.254, a link-local address that `is_global` calls `False`.

choices.text: The second lookup gives a different, internal address
choices.why: Right. Connect to the address that was checked, so a name that resolves differently the second time gains nothing.

choices.text: Checking the address instead of the name leaks it to the client
choices.why: The check happens on the server, and the client learns nothing from it.

choices.text: The check refuses `https`, so the download goes over plain HTTP
choices.why: The allowlist takes `https` as its one scheme.

prompt: What does `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'` do for a JSON API? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: An answer a browser ends up rendering as a page loads and runs nothing
choices.why: Right. JSON needs nothing, so forbidding everything costs nothing.

choices.text: No other site may put the answer inside a frame of its page
choices.why: Right. That is `frame-ancestors 'none'`.

choices.text: Programs such as curl cannot read the answer
choices.why: No header changes what a client written in code receives.

choices.text: Shared caches keep no copy of the answer
choices.why: That is `Cache-Control: no-store`.

choices.text: The browser does not guess that JSON is a script
choices.why: That is `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.
